content.text: Our nightly job that syncs users from Okta into our own database has started timing out. It used to take about four minutes and now it either takes forty minutes or it never finishes and gets killed by the scheduler at the one hour mark. Nothing in our code changed this week as far as I can tell. Where would you start?

A job that went from four minutes to forty without a code change usually means one of three things moved underneath it: the amount of data, the shape of a query, or a rate limit on the API you are pulling from.

Start by finding out which phase is slow. If the job logs timing per phase, pull last week and this week side by side. If it does not, the cheapest instrumentation is a timestamp before and after the fetch loop and before and after the write loop.

A few questions that would narrow it quickly:

- How many users does the sync pull now versus a month ago?
- Does it page through the Okta API, and if so what page size?
- Are the writes done one row at a time or in batches?

ok i added timing. the fetch loop is 90 seconds, basically unchanged. the write loop is the whole rest of it. we have 31k users now, we had about 28k a month ago so that grew a bit but not 10x.

writes are one at a time, it's a for loop doing an upsert per user. that's been like that since forever though

One upsert per user at 31k users means 31k round trips, and if each one now costs a little more than it used to, the total blows up while nothing looks obviously broken.

Two things to check on the write path:

First, what indexes are on the users table right now. Every index has to be maintained on every upsert, so an index somebody added recently for a dashboard query would tax all 31k writes.

Second, whether the upserts run inside one transaction or each in its own. Thirty-one thousand separate transactions each pay a commit.

someone added two indexes eight days ago. one of them is a gin index on a jsonb column called profile_attributes. that timing lines up almost exactly with when this started.

so is the fix just to drop the gin index? the dashboard person will not be happy but 40 minutes is not sustainable

Dropping it would fix the sync and break whatever query it was added for, so it is worth spending ten minutes before you do that.

A GIN index on jsonb is expensive to update, and by default Postgres buffers those updates in a pending list that gets flushed periodically, which makes the cost arrive in lumps rather than evenly. Check whether `fastupdate` is on for that index and what `gin_pending_list_limit` is set to.

The other angle is the write loop itself. Batching the upserts into groups of 500 with a single multi-row insert and an `on conflict` clause would cut round trips by a factor of 500, and the index maintenance would still happen but you would stop paying per-statement overhead 31 thousand times. That fix helps whether or not the index stays.

fastupdate is on, default limit. ok i'll try batching first since that doesn't require me to go argue with anyone. one thing i'm unsure about: if i batch the upserts into 500-row statements, what happens to my error handling? right now if one user fails to upsert i log it and continue with the rest. with a batch the whole statement fails and i lose the other 499, and honestly some of these records are dodgy, we get nulls in fields that are supposed to be required. how do people usually handle that
